summary: Specifies how an LDP speaker can signal that it has finished its initial label advertisements after a session starts. Without this, a peer cannot know when it has received all labels. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Label Distribution Protocol is how routers exchange labels for MPLS paths. This RFC adds a small message that lets one router tell its peer when it has sent all the labels it intends to send, so the peer can stop guessing.

questions: how does ldp signal label advertisement completion
what is end of lib in ldp
what is the unrecognized notification capability
subtitle: A way for Label Distribution Protocol peers to say when they have finished sending their labels.

tldr.problem: After an LDP session starts, one router cannot tell when its peer has finished sending every label binding it is going to send, so it has to guess.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Notification message carrying a new End-of-LIB status code and a Typed Wildcard FEC element, sent only after the peer has advertised a new Unrecognized Notification capability.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from August 2010 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It only helps in Downstream Unsolicited label advertisement mode, because in Downstream on Demand the speaker already knows when it has what it asked for.

facts.label: Status TLV flags
facts.value: The TLV E- and F-bits are set to zero

facts.label: Capability flags
facts.value: U must be 1, F must be 0, S must be 1

facts.label: Registration region
facts.value: Both code points are in the IETF Consensus range

today: RFC 5919 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It adds one status code and one capability to the Label Distribution Protocol, both from the IETF Consensus range.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
There are situations following LDP session establishment where it would be useful for an LDP speaker to know when its peer has advertised all of the labels from its Label Information Base (LIB).

One example is LDP-IGP synchronization, described in RFC 5443, where it would be useful for a speaker to know when its peer has completed advertisement of its IP label bindings. Another is LDP Graceful Restart, described in RFC 3478, where after an LDP session is re-established it would be helpful for each peer to signal the other after it has advertised all its label bindings.

The LDP specification, RFC 5036, provides no mechanism for an LDP speaker to notify a peer when it has completed its initial label advertisements to that peer. This document specifies the use of a Notification message with the End-of-LIB Status Code for exactly that purpose.

RFC 5036 implicitly assumes that new Status Codes will be defined over time, but it does not explicitly define the behaviour of an LDP speaker that does not understand a Status Code in a Notification message. To avoid backward compatibility problems, this document specifies the use of the LDP capability mechanism from RFC 5561 at session establishment time, so a peer can be told in advance that the sender is able to handle a Notification message carrying an unrecognized Status Code.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS routers swap labels so that traffic can take a fixed path through the network. The two ends of a session both hold labels, and one has no way to say that its part is done. This RFC gives it one.

sections.title: When the Mechanism Applies
sections.content:
The mechanisms in this document are deemed useful to LDP peering that uses the Downstream Unsolicited label advertisement mode of RFC 5036. In that mode a router pushes its label bindings to its peer without being asked.

They are not deemed useful to LDP peering that uses the Downstream on Demand label advertisement mode, because in that mode the LDP speaker requests particular label bindings from the peer anyway, and so knows when it has received them. There is nothing left to signal.
sections.plainLanguage: The signal only makes sense when a router pushes labels to its peer unasked. When a router asks for a specific label and waits for it, it already knows when the answer arrived.

sections.title: The Unrecognized Notification Capability
sections.content:
An LDP speaker may include a Capability Parameter, defined in RFC 5561, in the Initialization message to inform a peer that it ignores Notification messages that carry a Status Type-Length-Value (TLV) with a non-fatal Status Code unknown to it. That is the Unrecognized Notification capability.

The capability is a TLV with this layout: the U bit, the F bit, a 14-bit Unrecognized Notification field holding the value 0x0603, a 16-bit Length field, and then a byte holding the S bit followed by reserved bits. The U and F bits must be 1 and 0 respectively, as required by Section 3 of LDP Capabilities in RFC 5561. The S bit must be 1, which indicates that the capability is being advertised.

On receiving a Notification with an unrecognized Status Code, an LDP speaker may generate a console or system log message for troubleshooting.

IANA has assigned the Unrecognized Notification capability the code point 0x0603 from the TLV Type name space. RFC 5036 partitions that name space into three regions, and 0x0603 comes from the IETF Consensus range.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending the new message, a router advertises a capability in the opening handshake that says it can safely receive a status code it does not recognise. The capability is a small record with a type code of 0x0603 and a few flag bits.

sections.title: Signalling Completion of Label Advertisement
sections.content:
An LDP speaker that conforms to this specification should signal completion of its label advertisements to a peer by means of a Notification message, if its peer has advertised the Unrecognized Notification capability during session establishment. The speaker should send the Notification message per Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) Type even if it has zero label bindings to advertise to that peer.

The Notification message must carry two things. The first is a status TLV, with the TLV E- and F-bits set to zero, that carries the End-of-LIB Status Code, 0x0000002F. The second is a FEC TLV with the Typed Wildcard FEC element from RFC 5918, which identifies the FEC type for which the initial label advertisements have been completed. In the terms of Section 3.5.1 of RFC 5036, the FEC TLV is an optional parameter of the Notification message.

An LDP speaker must not send a Notification carrying the End-of-LIB Status Code to a peer unless that peer has advertised the Unrecognized Notification capability during session establishment. This applies to peers discovered by either the basic discovery or the extended discovery mechanism of Section 2.4 of RFC 5036.

IANA has assigned the End-of-LIB status code the code point 0x0000002F from the Status Code Name Space, which RFC 5036 partitions into an IETF Consensus region, a First Come First Served region and a Private Use region. The code point comes from the IETF Consensus range.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router has finished sending the labels it intends to send for one kind of traffic class, it sends a Notification that names the status code 0x0000002F and the traffic class it has finished. It may do this even when it had no labels to send at all.

sections.title: When the Notification Does Not Arrive
sections.content:
There is no guarantee that an LDP speaker will receive, or send, an End-of-LIB Notification from or to a peer even if the speaker has signalled the Unrecognized Notification capability. Although it is expected that a speaker supporting that capability would support sending and receiving an End-of-LIB Notification, it is not mandatory by definition. The RFC notes that this is not a concern, because a speaker would simply ignore a received Notification carrying an End-of-LIB status code, or any status code, that it does not recognise or support.

To deal with the possibility of a missing End-of-LIB Notification after session establishment, an LDP speaker may time out the receipt of an expected notification. A speaker should start a per-peer internal timer, called the EOL Notification timer, immediately following the LDP session establishment. The default value of 60 seconds is recommended, though the value should be configurable.

The timer is reset by each subsequent label advertisement and stopped by the End-of-LIB Notification message. Lacking any label advertisement from the peer, the timer would expire, causing the speaker to behave as if it had received the End-of-LIB notification from the peer. If the End-of-LIB Notification message is received after the timer has expired, the message should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A peer may simply never send the message, so each router also runs a 60 second timer per peer. The timer restarts every time a label arrives and stops when the end-of-LIB message arrives. If it runs out, the router assumes the peer finished, as if the message had arrived.

sections.title: Where the Notification Helps
sections.content:
The FECs known to an LDP speaker, and the labels the speaker has bound to those FECs, may change over time. That makes it hard to determine when a speaker has advertised all of its label bindings for a given FEC type, and in the end the determination is a judgment call the speaker makes. The speaker is assumed to know a set of FECs, depending on the label distribution control mode in use, Independent or Ordered, on the set of FECs to which it has bound local labels, and on configuration settings that may constrain which label bindings it may advertise to peers. From those it can work out the set of bindings for a given FEC type that it is permitted to advertise to a given peer.

Three situations benefit from the End-of-LIB Notification: LDP-IGP Sync, LDP Graceful Restart, and the response to a Wildcard Label Request from RFC 5918. In each of them, sending the notification after the speaker has completed its label binding advertisements makes the outcome deterministic instead of a guess.

LDP-IGP Sync. The synchronization mechanism in RFC 5443 lets directly connected LDP speakers delay the use of the link between them for transit IP traffic forwarding until the labels needed for IP-over-MPLS forwarding have been distributed and installed. Without the End-of-LIB Notification the speaker must rely on a heuristic to decide when it has received all of its peer's label bindings, and the heuristic chosen could cause LDP to signal the IGP too soon, which raises the likelihood that traffic is dropped, or too late, which keeps traffic on sub-optimal paths for longer than necessary. After receiving the notification, the speaker should consider LDP to be fully operational for the link and signal the IGP to start advertising the link with normal cost.

LDP Graceful Restart. Graceful Restart helps to reduce the loss of MPLS traffic caused by the restart of a router's LDP component. Without the End-of-LIB Notification, the restarting router and its peers consider the preserved forwarding state to be usable but stale until it is refreshed by new label advertisements following the re-establishment of LDP sessions, or until the configured time period expires, at which point any remaining stale forwarding state is removed. Receiving the notification lets a speaker stop using stale forwarding information learned from that peer and recover the resources it requires without waiting for the time period to expire. The time period expiry can still be used if the notification is not received.

Wildcard Label Request. When a speaker receives a Label Request message for a Typed Wildcard FEC, such as a particular FEC Element Type, it determines the set of bindings, according to any local filtering policy, to advertise for the FEC type named in the request. Assuming the peer advertised the Unrecognized Notification capability at session initialization, the speaker should send the peer an End-of-LIB Notification for that FEC type when it has completed advertisement of the permitted bindings. Receipt of the notification then removes the uncertainty about when the peer finished its advertisements for the requested Wildcard FEC Element Type.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things need to know when a peer has finished: keeping a link out of service until its labels are installed, clearing stale forwarding state after a router restart, and answering a request for every label of one kind. In all three cases the message replaces a guess with a fact.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: No security considerations beyond those that apply to the base LDP specification in RFC 5036, and that are further described in the security framework for MPLS and GMPLS networks in RFC 5920, apply to signalling the End-of-LIB condition.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC adds no security rules of its own. What applies to LDP generally applies here, because the new message travels over the same session as everything else.

items.title: LDP-IGP Sync
items.text: A link stays out of service for transit traffic until the labels it needs are installed, instead of a heuristic guess.

items.title: LDP Graceful Restart
items.text: Stale forwarding state learned from a peer can be dropped as soon as the peer says it has re-advertised everything.

items.title: Wildcard Label Request
items.text: A peer that asked for every label of one kind learns when the complete set has been sent.
